output.title: Exit plans get expensive when the workflow stays in your head
output.body:
If you ever think about selling, handing over, or simply stepping back from the business, the cost of an exit plan is not just legal fees or broker time. It is also the cost of every workflow you have not made visible yet.

For a small business owner, that usually shows up in the boring places: repeated customer questions, lead follow-up, invoice logging, and the one spreadsheet only you understand. The persona scenario Bareni works from is 8–10 hours a week of that kind of repetition. That is not a benchmark, just a useful warning light. If the work lives in your head, any exit plan has to pay to recover it later. That can mean more cleanup, more handover work, or more time spent training someone else.

The bounded decision is simple: pick one recurring task and ask whether it is repeatable enough to document before you automate it. If it is, Bareni’s normal sequence starts with a free 30-minute diagnostic to check whether AI fits that one workflow, then a one-page pilot proposal, then a paid MVP in days. Timings are intended scopes, not guarantees. Final approval stays human, especially for money movement or other high-risk decisions.

One practical next step: look at this week’s work log and mark the single task you would least want to explain from memory six months from now. That is probably the first exit-plan cost worth reducing.
